newsitem.title: USA: Wall St stocks seen opening mixed to lower.
newsitem.headline: Wall St stocks seen opening mixed to lower.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to open mixed to lower on a day dominated by economic data and earnings reports.

The Consumer Price Index and retail sales for December are due ahead of the opening bell, while Bay Networks Inc and Federal National Mortgage Association are among companies reporting quarterly results.
The most eagerly awaited earnings report is that of Intel Corp, due after the close of trading.

"I think we'll have a mixed opening because we had a mixed day yesterday. The oils were weak on Monday," said Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities. "Today will be colored by the CPI and retail sales, and there will be a lot of concentration on that Intel quarter."
Intel is expected to report fourth quarter earnings of $1.84 a share, up from $0.98 a year ago, according to First Call.
Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments, said Intel has nearly replaced International Business Machines Corp as a bellwether for high techs.

The market will also be looking at comments by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan in Belgium earlier today. He urged central banks not to take risks with inflation and said the best monetary policy was a steady course with the right amount of restraint. He warned against complacency in the fight against inflation despite recent success.
Cardillo said the speech indicated that "Greenspan believes we should be vigilant on inflation but there may not be a need to raise rates."
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average was down 26 points at 18,093.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was up 21 points at 4129.
Among U.S. shares traded in London, Intel was up 3/8 at 147-1/4.
The dollar recouped its early losses in Tokyo and was steady near session lows in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were thinly mixed, with the long bond down 2/32 to yield 6.86 percent.
The Wall Street Journal's "Heard on the Street" column says Chicago financier Sam Zell has an uphill struggle to form the largest single office REIT.

The New York Times's "Market Place" column says 1996 transformed how Americans think about mutual funds that invest in stocks. It quoted the Investment Company Institute as saying that such mutual funds received $233 billion in new cash from investors last year.
